newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Alliance H1 performance pleases market.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Alliance H1 performance pleases market.

text.p: Alliance & Leicester, the British building society-turned bank, posted its first set of results as a publicly listed company on Friday and confirmed it was still on the lookout for acquisitions.
The group passed its first test since flotation comfortably enough, beating market forecasts with first-half, pre-tax profits of 178 million pounds ($283 million), a fall of three percent.
The numbers included a 28 million pound charge for the costs of conversion.
While an acquisition remains a priority, A&L said it was not going to be rushed into a decision. However, an overseas purchase has been ruled out.

At its interim results last week the Woolwich described the possibility of UK acquisitions as problematic and said it may "cherry-pick" in France where it already has a foothold and where valuations are lower.
A&L, which converted to a bank on flotation in April, said its acquisition strategy was based on acquiring either more customers or more products to sell to existing customers.
Returning cash to shareholders remained an option, said finance director Richard Pym, but he refused to be committed to a timetable.

The Tier 1 capital ratio, which measures core capital against assets, weighted for risk, at 14 percent stands at nearly twice the industry average and acquisitions were the obvious way to bring that down, the company told analysts.

"Shareholders might prefer a buyback of shares but the company refuses to commit itself to a time frame on that. A&L clearly feels that the surplus capital is the passport to doing deals," said one analyst.
Pym said first half results showed there was capacity for both organic growth and lower capital ratios.
The better-than-expected profit figures are likely to lead to increased profit forecasts and A&L shares responded positively, adding 12-1/2 pence to 625 pence.
One supporter of the stock said the twin tracks of diversification of income away from mortgage lending and cost control, remained on track.

The company did caution that competition in both the core mortgage and savings markets had continued to put pressure on interest margins and one analyst said that the rapid growth in unsecured consumer lending could lead to worries about asset quality further down the line.
But analysts agreed that there remained scope for further cost-cutting and cross-selling of products.
The bank's target for the cost:income ratio is 55 percent against its current level of 61.6 percent.

Underlying operating profits rose seven percent to 206 million pounds in the first half while the dividend was raised by 18 percent to 6.4 pence per share, representing around one third of the expected dividend for the year.
While the company has seen some outflow of business since its conversion in April, windfall withdrawals have fallen significantly in the last few weeks .
Overall, customer accounts were almost identical to year-end -- less than 100 million pounds lower at 18.1 billion pounds.
Net mortgage lending increased sharply to 527 million pounds from 131 million pounds last year, a market share of 4.5 percent.
Staff reductions will continue in the second half though not at the rate in the first six months. In the past year, underlying staff levels have fallen by around 10 percent.
Jobs may go in a number of areas but the group is also expanding in insurance and leasing.
A&L recently launched in its own general insurance business which will be a core part of the product portfolio going forward.

Girobank produced level profit for the first half and the strategy remains to develop business within Girobank by selling specialist banking products to its existing customer base. ($ = 0.628 British Pounds)
